newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX volatilities narrowly mixed in U.S..
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX volatilities narrowly mixed in U.S..

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options were narrowly mixed in listless U.S. trading as spot drifted higher within familiar ranges, dealers said.

"The market's nervous but it's not going anywhere," said a trader at a European bank in New York. "There are not a lot of (option) buyers but it's choppy enough that there aren't a lot of sellers either."
A dominant view in the market appeared to be that spot would likely stay range-bound until the March 25 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, traders said.
But they added that longer-dated options were supported by views that volatility would eventually return later in the year, given the dollar's strong up moves earlier in the year.
The dollar/yen volatility curve steepened slightly as the dollar gradually rose above 123 yen, away from longstanding support around 120 yen, dealers said.
One-month dollar/yen implied volatility stood at 9.1/9.3 percent at U.S. midsession, off 0.2 point from late Wednesday levels. The back end was relatively steady, with one-year at 10.4/10.6.

Directional skews in dollar/yen option pricing were dissipating as spot has been drifting near the middle of a well-defined range -- between the high near 125 yen and the low just below 120 yen marked after the early-February meeting of Group of Seven industrial countries, traders said.
Risk reversals, which reflect pricing differential between puts and calls, stood at around par after being slightly in favor of yen puts for most of the recent weeks.
Traders noted that the range-trading environment has been prompting end-users to buy range binary, or knockout, options with barrier prices around 120 and 125 yen.
"If spot breaks through the 120 or 125 area, we'll probably have a lot of activity," a U.S. bank trader in California said.
But she added that as long as spot hovered at the present levels, the exotics would add to the downward pressure on volatilities.

Bank dealers who had sold knock-outs have steep time-decay positions and need to sell short-dated vanilla options. Once the barrier prices are broken and the exotics disappear, they must cover the shorts in the vanillas, bidding up front-end volatilities.
Dollar/mark volatilities were also generally steady, with the curve maintaining a positive slope it had regained earlier in the week when the dollar began pulling back.
Implied volatility for one-month dollar/mark stood at 9.3/9.5 percent, slightly above late Wednesday levels.
Traders noted that dollar/mark risk reversals, which had been skewed toward mark puts for some time, was now at around par.
"The dollar's trend seems to have taken a pause for the moment," the California trader said of the subdued bid for mark puts.
